questions.q: In the context of sparse and windowed attention, how is the attention mechanism modified to restrict which tokens attend to others?
options: By changing the formula QK^T/sqrt(d) to a linear projection.
By setting disallowed positions in the score matrix to -infinity before applying softmax.
By reducing the head dimension d to lower computational cost.
By removing the softmax function entirely to save memory.
questions.answer: By setting disallowed positions in the score matrix to -infinity before applying softmax.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'We do not change the formula QK^T/sqrt(d); we change what we feed into the softmax. We set disallowed positions to -infinity, so their weight becomes zero.'

questions.q: According to the lab analysis, why is the weight for token 0 in windowed attention (size 2) equal to 1?
options: Because token 0 attends to all 8 tokens in the sequence.
Because the mask logic for i=0 results in token 0 only attending to itself.
Because the window size is too large to include any other tokens.
Because sparse attention was applied instead of windowed attention.
questions.answer: Because the mask logic for i=0 results in token 0 only attending to itself.
questions.why: The lesson explains: 'For i=0, start=0. mask[0, 0:1] is True. So token 0 only attends to token 0. Thus, the weight is 1.'

questions.q: Which ComfyUI attention backend is described as implementing sub-quadratic attention for memory efficiency, where sparse/windowed logic often resides?
options: attention_basic
attention_flash
attention_sub_quad
ComfyAttention
questions.why: The lesson lists: 'attention_sub_quad: Implements sub-quadratic attention for memory efficiency. This is where sparse/windowed logic often lives, reducing the O(L^2) cost.'

questions.q: In the Trellis2 model, how does the concept of 'sparsity' differ from standard 2D models?
options: It uses a binary mask on a dense matrix to hide specific tokens.
It relies on a SparseTensor data structure where only non-zero voxels are processed.
It uses a larger window size to capture global context.
It removes all positional encodings to reduce computation.
questions.answer: It relies on a SparseTensor data structure where only non-zero voxels are processed.
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Here, the "sparsity" is not just a mask on a dense matrix, but a fundamental property of the SparseTensor data structure, where only non-zero voxels are processed.'

questions.q: Why is it a common mistake to assume that sparse attention is always faster than full dense attention?
options: Because sparse matrices require more memory to store the mask.
Because if hardware does not support sparse matrix multiplication efficiently, overhead can make it slower than a full dense matrix.
Because sparse attention requires recalculating the entire QK^T matrix twice.
Because sparse attention cannot be used with Flash Attention implementations.
questions.answer: Because if hardware does not support sparse matrix multiplication efficiently, overhead can make it slower than a full dense matrix.
questions.why: The lesson lists under common mistakes: 'If your hardware does not support sparse matrix multiplication efficiently, a dense matrix with many zeros might be slower than a full dense matrix due to overhead.'
